title: Epoch-based admission flow and attention preemptor for continuous batching
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Mixed workloads (short chat turns and long multi-token prefill requests) are creating pathological tails in our hosted API: short requests suffer high P95/P99 latency during prefill-heavy bursts because large prefill requests monopolize kernel slots and batch windows. Kernel selection heuristics currently operate per-batch and don’t reflect per-request deadline signals, so we see suboptimal kernel choices under heterogeneous mixes.

Goal: Implement an epoch-based admission controller paired with an attention preemptor so that short/latency-sensitive requests can be admitted to decode paths quickly without sacrificing total throughput. Integrate kernel selection hints into admission decisions so batches formed during each epoch are kernel-friendly and tail-latency aware.

High-level idea: Split the admission timeline into short epochs (10-50ms tunable). Each epoch collects candidates and makes admission/shaping decisions with a small optimizer that considers: per-request soft-deadline, estimated kernel cost (from profile), token-length distribution, and tenant fairness budgets. The attention preemptor allows an already-admitted prefill to yield partial GPU time / KV cache slices to a higher-priority decode when it can do so safely (using lightweight preemption points in the runtime). Kernel hints (fast/slow, memory-footprint category, quantization-sensitivity) are attached to requests and used by the epoch optimizer to create batch shapes that minimize cross-kernel contention and avoid pathological batch mixing.

Why different from previous batchers: instead of greedy queue-first admission, this ticket implements epoch-level planning with explicit preemption and kernel-aware shaping. The preemptor leverages attention-level checkpoints (KV cache snapshot points) rather than full request cancellation to preserve work and reduce wasted compute.

Success metrics: reduce P95 latency for short requests in mixed workloads by >=20% and P99 by >=15% without decreasing aggregate tokens/sec by more than 5% under steady-state traffic. No functional regressions for decoding correctness or streaming semantics.
acceptance_criteria: Internal canary shows >=20% improvement in P95 for short requests under synthetic mixed workload (short:50%, medium:30%, long:20%)
P99 improves by >=15% in the same scenario
Aggregate token throughput drop <=5% compared to baseline under steady-state
No increase in error-rate or malformed outputs for streaming and function-calling endpoints
Automated e2e regression suite (unit + perf) added to CI and green
Canary rollout plan defined and rollback safe-path implemented
design_decisions: Epoch length will be configurable; default 30ms. We picked epoch planning vs. per-request greedy admission to allow short-term global optimization rather than local heuristics.
Kernel hints are annotations from offline profiler (fast|balanced|memory) and will be augmented by real-time micro-profiling during warmup.
Attention preemption is implemented as cooperative preemption at KV cache boundaries: long prefill pauses at next safe checkpoint to allow short decode to run, then resumes.
Per-tenant soft budgets will be used to preserve fairness; tenants can opt into aggressive latency tiers to trade throughput for latency.
We will not perform preemption for sequences where preemption would violate strong ordering guarantees (e.g., multi-step tool calls) unless explicitly allowed by the client via header flag.
Kernel selection remains runtime-driven but receives a precomputed cost-estimate from the epoch optimizer; runtime retains final veto to avoid out-of-memory or kernel mismatch.
We choose to instrument minimal new API surface: admission hints are internal only; customers only see SLA/tier knobs in Console.
Fallback mode: if epoch optimizer fails or detects instability, system falls back to current greedy admission algorithm to avoid outages.
implementation_plan: Create feature branch 'epoch-admission-preemptor' and prototype optimizer as a library in infra/scheduler
Add kernel-hint metadata in request envelope and extend profiler to emit hint categories (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4521)
Implement epoch coordinator and admission optimizer (phase 1) with toggles behind runtime feature flag
Add cooperative attention preemptor in the serving runtime (phase 2) with unit tests for KV checkpoint correctness
Telemetry: add dashboards for P50/P95/P99 latency by request length, kernel mix, and epoch decisions
Integration tests + perf harness using synthetic mixed workloads (short/medium/long token mixes)
Internal canary for non-critical tenants, then staged rollout (10% -> 50% -> 100%) after success criteria met
test_plan: Unit tests for epoch optimizer logic and kernel-hint parsing
Runtime unit tests for attention preemption semantics and KV cache integrity
Perf tests: synthetic workload generator (repo: github.com/redwood-inference/perf-harness) with configurable mixes
Chaos tests: random preemption failures, injected kernel selection veto to ensure fallback works
Regression suite: verify long-running multi-step tool-call sessions are not broken
Canary monitoring: automated smoke checks and SLO alert hooks (Slack + PagerDuty)
rollout_plan: Merge behind feature flag and deploy to staging cluster
Run full perf suite and internal alpha for two days
Enable on 5% of hosted traffic (non-enterprise) for 24h, monitor dashboards and error budgets
If green, increase to 25% for 48h and run A/B comparison against baseline metrics
If green, increase to 100% with 8h monitoring window, otherwise rollback to greedy admission
Post-rollout: schedule retrospective and cost/latency analysis
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: Preemption adds overhead and might reduce throughput for long-only workloads. Mitigation: epoch optimizer detects long-only traffic and disables preemption, reverting to batch consolidation.
Risk: Incorrect kernel-hint leads to OOM or slow kernels. Mitigation: runtime kernel veto and conservative hint categories; monitor OOM and fallback quickly.
Risk: Complexity causes hard-to-debug tail cases. Mitigation: rich telemetry, request-level tracing (trace IDs survive preemption), and a fast rollback path.
Risk: Tenants with strict ordering requirements could be impacted. Mitigation: opt-out header and default conservative behavior for tool-call/transactional sessions.
